claim: The ascidian embryo is an ideal system to investigate how cell position is determined during embryogenesis.
source: The ascidian embryo is an ideal system to investigate how cell position is determined during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Spindles in every cell tend to align at metaphase in the long length of the apical surface except in cells undergoing unequal cleavage.
source: Using 3D timelapse imaging and computational methods we analyzed the planar cell divisions in ascidian early embryos and found that spindles in every cell tend to align at metaphase in the long length of the apical surface except in cells undergoing unequal cleavage.
evidence: This finding is based on 3D timelapse imaging and computational analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The invariant and conserved cleavage pattern of ascidian embryos consists in alternate planar cell divisions between ectoderm and endomesoderm.
source: Furthermore, the invariant and conserved cleavage pattern of ascidian embryos was found to consist in alternate planar cell divisions between ectoderm and endomesoderm.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis presented in the study.

claim: Abolishing cell cycle asynchrony consistently disrupted the spindle orienting mechanism underpinning the invariant cleavage pattern.
source: Crucially, abolishing cell cycle asynchrony consistently disrupted the spindle orienting mechanism underpinning the invariant cleavage pattern.
evidence: This is based on experimental manipulation of zygotic transcription and wee1 activity.

claim: A fate map for all chordate embryos at the blastula stage predicts that cells in different positions will give rise to new cell types and layers that are important for morphogenesis.
source: In chordate embryos the functional pattern of cells is generated before gastrulation such that a fate map for all chordate embryos at the blastula stage predicts that cells in different positions will give rise to new cell types and layers that are important for morphogenesis (Kourakis and Smith, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kourakis and Smith, 2005.

claim: Invertebrate chordate embryos of the ascidian display a similar fate map to other chordates even though their blastulae are composed of only 64 cells rather than several thousand cells typical of other chordates.
source: Invertebrate chordate embryos of the ascidian display a similar fate map to other chordates even though their blastulae are composed of only 64 cells rather than several thousand cells typical of other chordates (Kourakis and Smith, 2005; Lemaire et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kourakis and Smith, 2005 and Lemaire et al., 2008.

claim: Ascidian embryos display an invariant cleavage pattern with no cell migration or cell death up to the time of gastrulation.
source: Because ascidian embryos display an invariant cleavage pattern with no cell migration or cell death up to the time of gastrulation, cell division plane orientation is important for pattern formation (McDougall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McDougall et al., 2015.

claim: Cell division plane orientation is important for pattern formation in ascidian embryos.
source: Because ascidian embryos display an invariant cleavage pattern with no cell migration or cell death up to the time of gastrulation, cell division plane orientation is important for pattern formation (McDougall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the invariant cleavage pattern and supported by citation.

claim: All blastomeres are fate restricted in the 64 cell ascidian blastula.
source: All blastomeres are fate restricted in the 64 cell ascidian blastula and most cell divisions at the 32 cell stage are fate segregating asymmetric divisions (Lemaire et al., 2008; Lemaire, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lemaire et al., 2008 and Lemaire, 2009.

claim: Most cell divisions at the 32 cell stage are fate segregating asymmetric divisions.
source: All blastomeres are fate restricted in the 64 cell ascidian blastula and most cell divisions at the 32 cell stage are fate segregating asymmetric divisions (Lemaire et al., 2008; Lemaire, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lemaire et al., 2008 and Lemaire, 2009.

claim: The overall invariant temporal and spatial pattern of cell divisions in ascidians is conserved between distantly-related species.
source: The overall invariant temporal and spatial pattern of cell divisions in ascidians is even conserved between distantly-related species.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the introduction.

claim: Ascidians are split into three orders that diverged more than 350 millions years ago (aplousobranch, phlebobranch and stolidobranch).
source: Ascidians are split into three orders that diverged more than 350 millions years ago (aplousobranch, phlebobranch and stolidobranch), and it has been estimated that non-coding DNA sequences from two distinct ascidian species can be as different from each other as fish are from mammals (Stolfi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stolfi et al., 2014.

claim: Non-coding DNA sequences from two distinct ascidian species can be as different from each other as fish are from mammals.
source: Ascidians are split into three orders that diverged more than 350 millions years ago (aplousobranch, phlebobranch and stolidobranch), and it has been estimated that non-coding DNA sequences from two distinct ascidian species can be as different from each other as fish are from mammals (Stolfi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stolfi et al., 2014.

claim: The 24 cell stage embryo is common to both phlebobranch (Ciona/Phallusia) and stolidobranch (Halocynthia/Styela) ascidians.
source: Distantly-related species of ascidian also show the same relative cell cycle asynchrony since the 24 cell stage embryo is common to both phlebobranch (Ciona/Phallusia) and stolidobranch (Halocynthia/Styela) ascidians.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about conserved cell cycle asynchrony.

claim: In Phallusia, cell cycle asynchrony is induced by a GRN dependent upon nuclear accumulation of β-catenin in six vegetal cells of the 16 cell stage embryo.
source: In Phallusia this cell cycle asynchrony is induced by a GRN dependent upon nuclear accumulation of β-catenin in six vegetal cells of the 16 cell stage embryo (Dumollard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dumollard et al., 2013.

claim: β-catenin becomes nuclear in vegetal blastomeres in both Ciona and Halocynthia embryos at the 16 cell stage.
source: How such stereotyped cell cycle asynchrony has been conserved in distantly-related ascidians is presently unknown, but it is interesting to note that β-catenin becomes nuclear in vegetal blastomeres in both Ciona and Halocynthia embryos at the 16 cell stage (Kawai et al., 2007; Hudson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kawai et al., 2007 and Hudson et al., 2013.

claim: An underlying mechanism known as the long-axis rule based upon microtubule behavior and motors causes animal cell to divide orthogonal to their long axis.
source: For example, an underlying mechanism known as the long-axis rule based upon microtubule behavior and motors (reviewed in Minc and Piel, 2012) causes animal cell to divide orthogonal to their long axis as was noted more than a century ago by Hertwig (Hertwig, 1893).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Minc and Piel, 2012 and Hertwig, 1893.

claim: The geometric long-axis rule can be altered by cortical polarity cues such as lateral junctions or the apical cortex in asymmetrically dividing Drosophila neuroblasts.
source: This geometric long-axis rule can be altered by cortical polarity cues such as lateral junctions (Nakajima et al., 2013; Ragkousi and Gibson, 2014) or the apical cortex in asymmetrically dividing Drosophila neuroblasts (Siller and Doe, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakajima et al., 2013, Ragkousi and Gibson, 2014, and Siller and Doe, 2009.

claim: During planar cell divisions in epithelia and endothelia, a lateral belt of LGN/NuMA coupled with the exclusion of LGN/NuMA from the apical cortex causes planar spindle orientation.
source: During planar cell divisions in epithelia and endothelia, a lateral belt of LGN/NuMA coupled with the exclusion of LGN/NuMA from the apical cortex causes planar spindle orientation (Zheng et al., 2010; Morin and Bellaïche, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2010 and Morin and Bellaïche, 2011.

claim: Mitotic cell rounding does not seem to occur in the Xenopus blastula.
source: Mitotic cell rounding does not seem to occur in the Xenopus blastula (Strauss et al., 2006) and remains poorly documented in blastulae of other species (Xiong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strauss et al., 2006.

claim: A computational approach revealed that the first 4 cell divisions in ascidian embryos may follow a geometric rule in a similar manner to early Xenopus, Zebrafish or sea urchin embryos.
source: A computational approach revealed very recently that the first 4 cell divisions in ascidian embryos may follow a geometric rule in a similar manner to early Xenopus, Zebrafish or sea urchin embryos (Pierre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pierre et al., 2016.

claim: Major cell shape changes have been noted during the 32–44 cell stage in ascidian (Ciona) embryos.
source: Major cell shape changes have been noted during the 32–44 cell stage in ascidian (Ciona) embryos (Tassy et al., 2006) suggesting that mitotic cell rounding may occur in cells of the ascidian blastula.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tassy et al., 2006.

claim: At the 64 cell stage all cells of the ascidian blastula face the outside of the embryo.
source: At the 64 cell stage all cells of the ascidian blastula face the outside of the embryo (Figure 1A) suggesting that all cell divisions are parallel to the apical surface and that embryonic cleavage proceeds through planar cell divisions to generate the ascidian blastula.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: All cell divisions are parallel to the apical surface in ascidian embryos up to the 64 cell stage.
source: At the 64 cell stage all cells of the ascidian blastula face the outside of the embryo (Figure 1A) suggesting that all cell divisions are parallel to the apical surface and that embryonic cleavage proceeds through planar cell divisions to generate the ascidian blastula.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all cells face the outside at 64 cell stage.

claim: Three cells undergo OCD at the 16–24 cell stage (a5.3; a5.4; B5.2).
source: Using this strategy we could identify three cells undergoing OCD (asterisks in Figure 1A) at the 16–24 cell stage (a5.3; a5.4; B5.2) and seven cells at the 32–44 cell stage (A6.1; A6.2; a6.6; a6.7; a6.8; B6.2 and B6.3).
evidence: This is identified through analysis of cell division patterns shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Seven cells undergo OCD at the 32–44 cell stage (A6.1; A6.2; a6.6; a6.7; a6.8; B6.2 and B6.3).
source: Using this strategy we could identify three cells undergoing OCD (asterisks in Figure 1A) at the 16–24 cell stage (a5.3; a5.4; B5.2) and seven cells at the 32–44 cell stage (A6.1; A6.2; a6.6; a6.7; a6.8; B6.2 and B6.3).
evidence: This is identified through analysis of cell division patterns shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The square, T and linear patterns observed at the 64 cell stage are perfectly conserved in Styela partita and Ciona intestinalis.
source: Strikingly the square, T and linear patterns observed at the 64 cell stage are perfectly conserved in Styela partita (Figure 1B) and Ciona intestinalis (McDougall et al., 2015), showing that the pattern of planar cell divisions in early ascidian embryos may be perfectly conserved.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation to McDougall et al., 2015.

claim: Spindle rotation accompanies unequal cleavages in the germ lineage (B5.2; B63).
source: Time lapse imaging of mitotic spindles in live ascidian embryos revealed that spindle rotation accompanies unequal cleavages in the germ lineage (B5.2; B63; Prodon et al., 2010) but also in several other lineages where we predicted OCDs (for a5.3; b5.3; a6.6; a6.7; a6.8 see Video 1 and Figure 1C and for A6.1; A6.2 see Negishi and Yasuo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by time lapse imaging and citation to Prodon et al., 2010.

claim: Spindle rotation occurs in several lineages where OCDs were predicted (a5.3; b5.3; a6.6; a6.7; a6.8; A6.1; A6.2).
source: Time lapse imaging of mitotic spindles in live ascidian embryos revealed that spindle rotation accompanies unequal cleavages in the germ lineage (B5.2; B63; Prodon et al., 2010) but also in several other lineages where we predicted OCDs (for a5.3; b5.3; a6.6; a6.7; a6.8 see Video 1 and Figure 1C and for A6.1; A6.2 see Negishi and Yasuo, 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Video 1, Figure 1C, and supported by citation to Negishi and Yasuo, 2015.

claim: Blastomeres not displaying OCD such as b6.8 blastomeres show no major spindle rotation.
source: In contrast, blastomeres not displaying OCD such as b6.8 blastomeres show no major spindle rotation (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: At prophase/prometaphase, apical cell geometry poorly predicts spindle orientation in a6.6 and a6.8 (orienting deviation: 61.0° in a6.6 and 47.0° in a6.8).
source: By comparing the angle between the observed and predicted spindle orientations (orienting deviation) it can be observed that at prophase/prometaphase (i.e., before spindle rotation), apical cell geometry poorly predicts spindle orientation in a6.6 and a6.8 (orienting deviation: 61.0° in a6.6 and 47.0° in a6.8) whereas apical cell geometry predicts reliably spindle position in b6.8 (orienting deviation: 14.7°).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and measurement of orienting deviation.

claim: At metaphase, all observed spindles show an orienting deviation of less than 20° indicating that apical cell shape predicts reliably spindle orientation in the apical plane.
source: In contrast, at metaphase, all observed spindles show an orienting deviation of less than 20° indicating that apical cell shape predicts reliably spindle orientation in the apical plane (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Compressing the 4 cell stage embryo along the Animal-Vegetal axis creates a flattened embryo which, upon cell division, gives rise to a single layer of 8 cells.
source: Compressing the 4 cell stage embryo along the Animal-Vegetal axis creates a flattened embryo (Figure 2A, '4-cell compressed') which, upon cell division, gives rise to a single layer of 8 cells.
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figure 2A.

claim: Computational analysis shows a good prediction of spindle positioning by cell shape in compressed embryos (orienting deviation: 22.7 ± 5.6° for A3 blastomere and 19.5 ± 3.4° for B3).
source: Computational analysis shows a good prediction of spindle positioning by cell shape in these embryos (orienting deviation: 22.7 ± 5.6° for A3 blastomere and 19.5 ± 3.4° for B3) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling of compressed embryos shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Downregulating cell adhesion causes embryonic morphologies at the 8 cell stage ranging from wild type patterns (2 layers of 4 cells) to one layer of 8 cells with all intermediate patterns.
source: For example, downregulating cell adhesion causes embryonic morphologies at the 8 cell stage ranging from wild type patterns (2 layers of 4 cells) to one layer of 8 cells with all intermediate patterns (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Cell shape can orient spindle positioning in early ascidian embryos.
source: These observations show that cell shape can orient spindle positioning in early ascidian embryos and indicates that cell adhesion and regulated apicobasal polarity are absolutely vital to maintain the cell shapes supporting the invariant cleavage pattern of early ascidian embryos.
evidence: This is concluded from the compression and cell adhesion experiments.

claim: Cell adhesion and regulated apicobasal polarity are absolutely vital to maintain the cell shapes supporting the invariant cleavage pattern of early ascidian embryos.
source: These observations show that cell shape can orient spindle positioning in early ascidian embryos and indicates that cell adhesion and regulated apicobasal polarity are absolutely vital to maintain the cell shapes supporting the invariant cleavage pattern of early ascidian embryos.
evidence: This is concluded from the compression and cell adhesion experiments.

claim: Sphericity of blastomeres at metaphase was found to be significantly different from a round standard from the 4 cell stage.
source: Sphericity of blastomeres at metaphase was found to be significantly different from a round standard from the 4 cell stage and was particularly pronounced at the 16–24 and 32–44 cell stages during which spindle rotations occur (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At the 32 cell stage, in silico isolated blastomeres were found to be columnar during interphase and to flatten along the apical direction at metaphase.
source: At the 32 cell stage, in silico isolated blastomeres were found to be columnar during interphase and to flatten along the apical direction at metaphase (Figure 3B) without significantly changing cell volume (data not shown).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through 3D rendering analysis.

claim: A large increase in apical surface area accompanies mitotic cell rounding (from 0,15–0,23 at interphase to 0,42–0,56 at metaphase).
source: We then segmented manually apical (red) from basolateral (green) membranes on each 3D-rendered blastomere and calculated the apical surface ratio (apical surface divided by total surface) and found that a large increase in apical surface area accompanies mitotic cell rounding (from 0,15–0,23 at interphase to 0,42–0,56 at metaphase, Figure 3B) similarly to what is observed in differentiated epithelia (Ragkousi and Gibson, 2014).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 3B, with comparison to Ragkousi and Gibson, 2014.

claim: 88% of cells show an orienting deviation of 30° or less.
source: In our data set, 88% of cells show an orienting deviation of 30° or less, 78% of cells have an orienting deviation under 20° and 52% of cells show an orienting deviation of less than 10° (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is quantified from the data set and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 78% of cells have an orienting deviation under 20°.
source: In our data set, 88% of cells show an orienting deviation of 30° or less, 78% of cells have an orienting deviation under 20° and 52% of cells show an orienting deviation of less than 10° (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is quantified from the data set and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 52% of cells show an orienting deviation of less than 10°.
source: In our data set, 88% of cells show an orienting deviation of 30° or less, 78% of cells have an orienting deviation under 20° and 52% of cells show an orienting deviation of less than 10° (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is quantified from the data set and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Spindle orientation could not be predicted reliably in B5.2, B6.3 and A6.3 blastomeres (i.e. orienting deviation is above 30°).
source: In contrast spindle orientation could not be predicted reliably in B5.2, B6.3 and A6.3 blastomeres (i. e. orienting deviation is above 30°) suggesting that in these three blastomeres apical cell shape does not regulate spindle positioning in the apical plane.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and measurement of orienting deviation.

claim: The CAB is a cortical complex composed of cell polarity proteins.
source: The CAB is a cortical complex composed of cell polarity proteins (Patalano et al., 2006) which is segregated in the germ lineage and is responsible for spindle orientation in the B5.2/B6.3 mitoses in a cell autonomous manner (Nishikata et al., 1999; Prodon et al., 2010) against apical cell shape (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Patalano et al., 2006.

claim: The CAB is responsible for spindle orientation in the B5.2/B6.3 mitoses in a cell autonomous manner against apical cell shape.
source: The CAB is a cortical complex composed of cell polarity proteins (Patalano et al., 2006) which is segregated in the germ lineage and is responsible for spindle orientation in the B5.2/B6.3 mitoses in a cell autonomous manner (Nishikata et al., 1999; Prodon et al., 2010) against apical cell shape (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishikata et al., 1999 and Prodon et al., 2010, and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Zygotic transcription is required for germ layer patterning starting from the 16 cell stage in ascidians.
source: Conversely, zygotic transcription is required for germ layer patterning starting from the 16 cell stage in ascidians (Lemaire, 2009; Hudson et al., 2013) and also for generating cell cycle asynchrony from the 16 cell stage (Dumollard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lemaire, 2009 and Hudson et al., 2013.

claim: Zygotic transcription is required for generating cell cycle asynchrony from the 16 cell stage.
source: Conversely, zygotic transcription is required for germ layer patterning starting from the 16 cell stage in ascidians (Lemaire, 2009; Hudson et al., 2013) and also for generating cell cycle asynchrony from the 16 cell stage (Dumollard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dumollard et al., 2013.

claim: Removing the CP prevents unequal cleavage in CAB-containing blastomeres at the 8 cell stage (B4.1 pair) resulting in more centered spindles.
source: For example, removing the CP prevents unequal cleavage in CAB-containing blastomeres at the 8 cell stage (B4.1 pair) resulting in more centered spindles (Figure 5B) and the absence of small cells in the vegetal posterior pole of the embryo of CP-ablated embryos (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The activity of the maternal CAB impacts not only unequal cleavage in the germ lineage but also cell shape and hence cell divisions in the rest of the embryo.
source: Therefore, the activity of the maternal CAB impacts not only unequal cleavage in the germ lineage but also cell shape and hence cell divisions in the rest of the embryo.
evidence: This is concluded from the CP-ablation experiments.

claim: All mitotic spindle rotations previously observed at the 16 and 32 cell stages are strongly impaired in Pem1 and DN-Tcf expressing embryos resulting in cell divisions with different orientation from the invariant cleavage pattern.
source: However, all mitotic spindle rotations previously observed at the 16 and 32 cell stages are strongly impaired in Pem1 and DN-Tcf expressing embryos resulting in cell divisions with different orientation from the invariant cleavage pattern (termed 'misoriented cell divisions') (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: The blastomeres undergoing spindle rotation displayed more occurrence of misoriented cell divisions (a5.3, b5.3, A6.1, A6.2, a6.6, a6.7, a6.8) in embryos expressing Pem1 or DN-Tcf.
source: Counting the occurrence of misoriented cell divisions in embryos expressing Pem1 or DN-Tcf (Figure 6B) shows that the blastomeres undergoing spindle rotation displayed more occurrence of misoriented cell divisions (a5.3, b5.3, A6.1, A6.2, a6.6, a6.7, a6.8 marked with an asterisk in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is quantified and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Misoriented cell divisions in manipulated embryos are still predicted reliably by apical cell shape.
source: The shape of the apical surface appears altered both in Pem1 and DN-Tcf expressing embryos and computational analysis of cell divisions in a6.8 (normally displaying spindle rotation) shows that misoriented cell divisions are still predicted reliably by apical cell shape (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown through computational analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: Wee1 maternal RNAs are present in the unfertilized oocyte in Phallusia mammillata.
source: Wee1 maternal RNAs are present in the unfertilized oocyte in Phallusia mammillata (Figure 7A, see also RNA-seq data in Aniseed database: http://www.aniseed.cnrs.fr/ with Gene Id: phmamm.CG.MTP2014.S423.g08568) where it is enriched in the vegetal cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Maternal Wee1 transcripts are enriched in the vegetal cortex of the unfertilized oocyte.
source: Wee1 maternal RNAs are present in the unfertilized oocyte in Phallusia mammillata (Figure 7A, see also RNA-seq data in Aniseed database: http://www.aniseed.cnrs.fr/ with Gene Id: phmamm.CG.MTP2014.S423.g08568) where it is enriched in the vegetal cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Zygotic Wee1 transcripts first appear at late 32 cell stage in the endoderm lineage (64–76-stage) just before these cells invaginate.
source: Zygotic Wee1 transcripts first appear at late 32 cell stage in the endoderm lineage (64–76-stage) just before these cells invaginate.
evidence: This is stated based on in situ hybridization results.

claim: After the onset of gastrulation (112 cell stage) Wee1 transcripts are expressed in mesodermal cells just before they invaginate.
source: After the onset of gastrulation (112 cell stage) Wee1 transcripts are expressed in mesodermal cells just before they invaginate (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Wee1 inhibition speeded up the slow cell cycle in the ectoderm at the 16 cell stage without affecting the cell cycle duration of the vegetal endomesoderm thereby eliminating the transient 24 cell stage.
source: We modified Wee1 activity in the whole embryo (see Materials and methods, Murakami et al., 2004; Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014) and found, as anticipated, that Wee1 inhibition speeded up the slow cell cycle in the ectoderm at the 16 cell stage without affecting the cell cycle duration of the vegetal endomesoderm thereby eliminating the transient 24 cell stage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figure 7B.

claim: At the 32 cell stage, cell cycle asynchrony between ectoderm (animal) and endomesoderm (vegetal) was 6–8 min in Wee1-manipulated embryos compared to 15 min in control embryos.
source: At the 32 cell stage, cell cycle asynchrony between ectoderm (animal) and endomesoderm (vegetal) was 6–8 min in Wee1-manipulated embryos compared to 15 min in control embryos (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The blastomeres most affected by synchronization were the ones displaying oriented cell division (b5.3, A6.1, A6.2, a6.7 and a6.8) or daughters of cells displaying OCD (ie b6.5, b6.6).
source: Therefore the blastomeres most affected by synchronization were the ones displaying oriented cell division (b5.3, A6.1, A6.2, a6.7 and a6.8) or daughters of cells displaying OCD (ie b6.5, b6.6).
evidence: This is concluded from counting misoriented cell divisions in Wee1-manipulated embryos.

claim: Inhibition of cell cycle asynchrony did not seem to disrupt the mechanisms supporting spindle orientation in the apical plane.
source: Therefore, inhibition of cell cycle asynchrony did not seem to disrupt the mechanisms supporting spindle orientation in the apical plane and misoriented cell divisions may rather be due to altered apical surface area.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that misoriented divisions still align with the long axis of the apical surface.

claim: Apical cell shape is a major driver of cell positioning in the ascidian blastula.
source: Thus we argue that, together with apico-basal polarity which likely enforces the planar orientation of cell division, apical cell shape is a major driver of cell positioning in the ascidian blastula.
evidence: This is argued based on the computational modeling results.

claim: Cell cycle asynchrony impacts the spatial pattern of planar cell divisions by regulating the shape of the cell's apical surface at metaphase.
source: We suggest that cell cycle asynchrony impacts the spatial pattern of planar cell divisions by regulating the shape of the cell's apical surface at metaphase.
evidence: This is suggested based on the experimental results.

claim: The zygotic GRN driven by nuclear β-catenin that patterns germ layers is also responsible for causing cell cycle asynchrony, which in turn enforces the invariant cleavage pattern through cell shape dependent mitotic spindle orientation in the apical plane at the 16-32-44-cell stages.
source: Therefore the zygotic GRN driven by nuclear β-catenin that patterns germ layers is also responsible for causing cell cycle asynchrony, which in turn enforces the invariant cleavage pattern through cell shape dependent mitotic spindle orientation in the apical plane at the 16-32-44-cell stages.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental manipulations of β-catenin and cell cycle timing.

claim: Entry into mitosis is accompanied with partial cell rounding via apical expansion (and hence a reduction in cell adhesion) in the ascidian blastula.
source: We find here that entry into mitosis is accompanied with partial cell rounding via apical expansion (and hence a reduction in cell adhesion) in the ascidian blastula.
evidence: This is observed through 3D rendering and analysis of cell shape changes.

claim: The overall cell cycle asynchrony between the animal and vegetal cells is about 15 min which is about the duration of M phase.
source: It is interesting to note that the overall cell cycle asynchrony between the animal and vegetal cells is about 15 min. which is about the duration of M phase.
evidence: This is noted from the timing measurements.

claim: Both phlebobranchs and stolidobranchs ascidians display nuclear β-catenin in vegetal cells at the 16 cell stage.
source: Indeed, both phlebobranchs and stolidobranchs ascidians display nuclear β-catenin in vegetal cells at the 16 cell stage (Ciona: Hudson et al. (2013), Halocynthia: Kawai et al., 2007), and it is a GRN controlled by β-catenin that causes cell cycle asynchrony starting at the 16 cell stage (Dumollard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hudson et al., 2013, Kawai et al., 2007, and Dumollard et al., 2013.

claim: Unequal cleavage of the two vegetal posterior blastomeres at the 16 cell stage affects the shape of every cell in the early embryo.
source: Unequal cleavage of the two vegetal posterior blastomeres at the 16 cell stage thus affects the shape of every cell in the early embryo.
evidence: This is concluded from the CP-ablation experiments.

claim: Regulated apicobasal polarity is crucial to maintain cell adhesion in the ascidian embryo to propagate individual cell deformations to the rest of the embryo and implement the invariant cleavage pattern.
source: It is noteworthy that regulated apicobasal polarity is crucial to maintain cell adhesion in the ascidian embryo to propagate individual cell deformations to the rest of the embryo and implement the invariant cleavage pattern.
evidence: This is concluded from the cell adhesion and polarity manipulation experiments.
